faq.q: What is a CBC test and why is it done?
faq.a: A Complete Blood Count (CBC) measures red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. It is done to detect anemia, check for infections, monitor treatment response, and assess general health.

faq.q: Is fasting required for a CBC test?
faq.a: No, fasting is not required for a standard CBC test. You can eat and drink normally before sample collection.

faq.q: What does a low platelet count in CBC indicate?
faq.a: A low platelet count (thrombocytopenia) can be caused by viral infections like dengue, immune disorders, medications, or bone marrow conditions. A medical doctor should review low platelet counts promptly.

faq.q: How soon will I get my CBC test results?

faq.q: Should I take my thyroid medication before the blood test?
faq.a: Most endocrinologists advise having your blood sample drawn in the morning before taking your daily thyroid tablet. Confirm with your doctor.

faq.q: What is considered a normal HbA1c level?
faq.a: Below 5.7% is considered normal. An HbA1c between 5.7% and 6.4% indicates prediabetes, while 6.5% or higher on two separate tests indicates diabetes.

faq.q: Do I need to fast for an HbA1c test?
faq.a: No, fasting is not required for an HbA1c test. You can take the test at any time of the day regardless of when you ate.

faq.q: How often should a diabetic person check their HbA1c?
faq.a: Diabetic individuals should generally test their HbA1c every 3 months if blood sugar is fluctuating, or every 6 months if sugar levels are stable.

faq.a: A 25-OH Vitamin D level between 30 to 100 ng/mL is optimal. Levels between 20-30 ng/mL represent insufficiency, while below 20 ng/mL indicates deficiency.

faq.q: What are common signs of Vitamin D deficiency?

faq.a: Yes, an overnight fast of 10 to 12 hours is recommended to obtain accurate bilirubin and liver enzyme readings.

faq.q: Can fatty liver be detected with an LFT?
faq.a: Yes, elevated liver enzymes (SGPT/SGOT) are often the first laboratory indicator of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

faq.q: Why is KFT test important for diabetic and high BP patients?
faq.a: Diabetes and hypertension are the two leading causes of chronic kidney disease. Routine KFT testing allows early detection and management to protect renal health.

faq.a: Eating before the test directly increases blood triglyceride levels and alters LDL calculations, producing false high results. Only water is permitted during fasting.

faq.q: What is the difference between HDL and LDL cholesterol?
faq.a: HDL is 'good' cholesterol because it removes excess cholesterol from arteries back to the liver. LDL is 'bad' cholesterol because it deposits plaque inside artery walls.

faq.a: A high CRP indicates significant acute inflammation in your body, which could be from a bacterial infection, pneumonia, autoimmune condition, or cardiovascular inflammation.

faq.a: CRP rises and falls much faster in response to inflammation than ESR, providing a more immediate snapshot of your current inflammatory state.

faq.a: Serum iron fluctuates daily based on meals. Ferritin reflects your body's total deep iron storage reserves, detecting iron deficiency weeks before anemia appears in a CBC.

faq.q: Can I drink plain water during fasting before a blood test?

keyPoints: Hemoglobin: Normal range is 13.5 - 17.5 g/dL for men, 12.0 - 15.5 g/dL for women. Low levels indicate anemia.
Platelet Count: Normal range is 150,000 to 450,000 per mcL. Levels below 100,000 require prompt medical evaluation.
Total Leukocyte Count (TLC): Normal range is 4,000 to 11,000 cells/mcL. High TLC indicates active infection or inflammation.
Differential WBC: Neutrophils fight bacteria; Lymphocytes combat viral infections; Eosinophils respond to allergies.
RBC Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC): Help distinguish between iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia, and B12 deficiency.

faq.q: What causes high white blood cells (leukocytosis) on a CBC?
faq.a: Elevated WBC counts most commonly indicate your immune system is actively fighting a bacterial infection, tissue injury, physical stress, or an inflammatory condition.

faq.q: What is the danger level for low platelets?
faq.a: While normal platelets are 150,000+, medical concern increases below 50,000, and levels under 20,000 pose significant spontaneous bleeding risks requiring urgent hospital care.

faq.q: Can prediabetes with an HbA1c of 6.2% be reversed?

faq.q: Why is my daily fasting sugar normal but my HbA1c high?
faq.a: Fasting blood sugar measures a single morning moment. If your blood sugar spikes significantly after lunch, dinner, or snacks, your 3-month average HbA1c will be high even if morning fasting readings look fine.

faq.a: An SGPT of 75 indicates mild to moderate liver cell irritation, most commonly due to fatty liver or medication. While not an emergency, it is a warning sign that requires dietary adjustment, weight loss, and medical follow-up.

faq.q: Can drinking coffee help reduce liver enzymes?

faq.q: Why does high TSH mean low thyroid function?
faq.a: Think of TSH as an accelerator pedal. When your thyroid is sluggish and producing too little hormone, your brain presses the pedal harder by pumping out more TSH to stimulate it.

faq.q: What TSH level requires medication?
faq.a: Doctors typically initiate thyroxine medication when TSH exceeds 10 mIU/L, or between 4.5 and 10 if symptoms, high cholesterol, thyroid antibodies, or pregnancy are present.

articles.overview: Heart disease is often silent until a major event occurs. A Lipid Profile test provides an essential roadmap of your cardiovascular health. Learn the critical differences between good and bad cholesterol, why triglycerides matter, and how to improve your numbers naturally.
keyPoints: Total Cholesterol: Desirable level is under 200 mg/dL
LDL Cholesterol ('Bad'): Target under 100 mg/dL (under 70 mg/dL for high-risk cardiac patients)
HDL Cholesterol ('Good'): Target above 40 mg/dL for men and above 50 mg/dL for women
Triglycerides: Desirable level under 150 mg/dL (closely linked to dietary carbs and sugar)
Diet: Avoid trans fats, bakery items, and palm oil; eat more oats, flaxseeds, almonds, and soluble fiber

faq.q: How can I raise my good HDL cholesterol?
faq.a: Regular aerobic exercise (brisk walking 30 minutes daily), consuming omega-3 fatty acids, quitting smoking, and eating nuts like walnuts and almonds are the most effective ways to raise HDL.

faq.q: Why are high triglycerides so common in India?
faq.a: High triglycerides in Indian diets are largely driven by high consumption of refined carbohydrates (white rice, maida, sweets) and fried snacks, combined with a sedentary lifestyle.

articles.h1: Kidney Function Test (KFT): Creatinine Normal Ranges & Signs
articles.title: Serum Creatinine Normal Range & Kidney Function Guide | Healthians
articles.description: Understanding your Kidney Function Test (KFT). Learn normal Serum Creatinine, Blood Urea & eGFR ranges, early kidney warning signs, and prevention tips.
articles.schemaDesc: Medical guide to interpreting Kidney Function Test (KFT) markers, serum creatinine levels, and glomerular filtration health.
articles.overview: Your kidneys filter over 180 liters of blood daily, eliminating toxins while conserving essential minerals. Unfortunately, chronic kidney disease can progress silently until over 60% of kidney function is lost. Learning to interpret your KFT report is vital for protecting your renal longevity.
keyPoints: Serum Creatinine: Normal range is 0.7 to 1.3 mg/dL for men, 0.5 to 1.1 mg/dL for women
Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN): Normal range is 7 to 20 mg/dL
eGFR (estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate): Above 90 mL/min is optimal; below 60 suggests chronic kidney disease
Warning signs: Swelling in ankles or under eyes (edema), frothy urine, fatigue, metallic taste in mouth
Protection: Control blood pressure under 130/80, maintain HbA1c under 7.0%, and stay well-hydrated

faq.q: Can high creatinine be caused by muscle building or gym protein?
faq.a: Yes, high muscle mass and creatine monohydrate supplements can mildly elevate blood creatinine without kidney disease. A Cystatin-C test can provide an accurate kidney evaluation independent of muscle mass.

faq.q: How can I naturally lower my creatinine levels?
faq.a: Stay adequately hydrated, avoid over-the-counter NSAID painkillers (like ibuprofen), manage blood pressure and blood sugar strictly, and reduce excessive red meat consumption.

articles.overview: High uric acid (hyperuricemia) occurs when your body either produces too much uric acid or your kidneys cannot excrete it quickly enough. Over time, sharp urate crystals accumulate in joint tissues, causing severe inflammatory attacks of gout, typically striking the big toe or ankles at night.
keyPoints: Normal uric acid range: 3.5 - 7.2 mg/dL for men, 2.6 - 6.0 mg/dL for women
Symptoms: Sudden, intense burning and swelling in big toe, ankle, or knee
Foods to avoid: Red meat, organ meats, beer, alcohol, shellfish, and sugary sodas containing high-fructose corn syrup
Foods that help: Cherries, lemon water, low-fat curd, cucumbers, and drinking 3+ liters of water daily
High uric acid can also form painful kidney stones

faq.q: Can high uric acid cause joint pain without redness?
faq.a: Yes, chronic mild hyperuricemia can cause persistent aching in joints, heels, and ankles even without the dramatic swelling of an acute gout flare.

faq.q: Does drinking lemon water really reduce uric acid?
faq.a: Yes! Fresh lemon juice stimulates the production of calcium carbonate in the body, which helps neutralize uric acid and encourages urinary excretion.

articles.overview: C-Reactive Protein (CRP) is an acute-phase reactant synthesized by the liver. When tissues in your body experience acute bacterial invasion, viral trauma, or autoimmune flare-ups, liver cells flood the bloodstream with CRP. Discover how doctors interpret this critical diagnostic signal.
keyPoints: Normal standard CRP is under 5.0 to 6.0 mg/L (or under 10 mg/L in some labs)
Mild elevation (10 - 40 mg/L): Viral infections, mild inflammation, pregnancy, or obesity
Moderate to severe elevation (40 - 200 mg/L): Acute bacterial infection, pneumonia, or severe autoimmune flares
Very high (>200 mg/L): Severe systemic bacterial sepsis or major trauma
High-Sensitivity CRP (Hs-CRP) measures tiny cardiac risk elevations below 3.0 mg/L

faq.q: How quickly does CRP drop after an infection is treated?
faq.a: CRP has a short half-life of roughly 19 hours. Once the underlying bacterial or viral infection resolves, CRP drops rapidly back toward baseline within a few days.

faq.q: Can stress or exercise elevate CRP?
faq.a: Intense, exhausting physical exertion can temporarily cause a mild increase in CRP due to transient muscle fiber micro-trauma, but mental stress alone does not cause significant spikes.

articles.name: Difference Between Fasting Blood Sugar and HbA1c Test
articles.h1: Fasting Blood Sugar vs HbA1c: Key Differences Explained
articles.title: Fasting Blood Sugar vs HbA1c: Which Test is Better? | Healthians
articles.description: Confused between Fasting Sugar and HbA1c? Learn how these two tests differ, why doctors order both, and which test is more reliable for diabetes.
articles.schemaDesc: Comparative medical guide explaining the diagnostic roles, physiological differences, and clinical utility of Fasting Glucose vs Glycated Hemoglobin.
articles.overview: Both Fasting Blood Sugar (FBS) and HbA1c measure blood glucose, yet they often yield seemingly contradictory results. One can be normal while the other is elevated. This comprehensive comparison explains why both tests are complementary and essential for mastering diabetes control.
keyPoints: Time window: Fasting sugar captures a single instant (morning baseline). HbA1c captures a 90-day moving average.
Fasting requirement: FBS requires 8-10 hours strict fasting. HbA1c requires zero fasting.
Daily fluctuation: FBS is heavily influenced by last night's dinner, stress, and sleep quality. HbA1c ignores daily fluctuations.
Diagnosis: Both tests are recognized by international diabetes associations; using both together prevents false negatives.
Post-meal spikes: A patient with normal fasting sugar can still have an elevated HbA1c if post-meal sugars spike during the day.

faq.q: Can I just do an HbA1c test and skip fasting blood sugar?
faq.a: While HbA1c is a superior long-term marker, fasting blood sugar shows your true basal hepatic glucose output. Doctors prefer checking both together for complete diagnostic clarity.

faq.q: Can severe anemia distort HbA1c results?
faq.a: Yes. Conditions that alter red blood cell lifespan—such as severe iron deficiency anemia or hemolytic anemia—can cause artificially elevated or lowered HbA1c readings.

articles.overview: Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs) are among the most frequent bacterial infections, particularly among women. From mild bladder irritation (cystitis) to severe kidney infections (pyelonephritis), prompt diagnosis via a simple Urine Routine & Microscopy test is key to fast relief and preventing kidney damage.
keyPoints: Common symptoms: Burning sensation during urination (dysuria), constant urgency, cloudy or foul-smelling urine, and lower pelvic pressure
Pus cells (Leukocytes): Normal is 0-5 per high power field. Higher counts indicate active bacterial infection
Nitrites & Bacteria: Positive nitrites strongly point to gram-negative bacterial infection like E. coli
Microscopic Hematuria: Trace red blood cells indicate inflamed bladder lining
Clean-catch midstream collection prevents contamination from external skin flora

faq.q: How soon should a UTI be treated?
faq.a: A UTI should be evaluated by a doctor promptly. Unchecked bladder infections can ascend upward through the ureters into the kidneys, causing serious pyelonephritis with high fever and back pain.

faq.q: Why are women significantly more prone to UTIs than men?
faq.a: Women have a much shorter urethra located closer to the rectal area, allowing bacteria like E. coli to reach the bladder more easily.

articles.overview: Iron deficiency anemia is the most prevalent nutritional deficiency in India, affecting over 50% of women and young children. keyPoints: Symptoms: Chronic fatigue, paleness under eyelids, brittle spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), shortness of breath climbing stairs, and hair fall
CBC indicators: Low Hemoglobin, low MCV (microcytic), and low MCH (hypochromic)
Ferritin test: The most sensitive indicator of deep iron stores. Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency even if hemoglobin is borderline
Indian dietary sources: Spinach (palak), beetroot, pomegranate, lentils, dates, jaggery, roasted chana, and chicken/fish
Absorption booster: Always pair iron-rich meals with Vitamin C (lemon juice, amla, oranges) to double iron absorption

faq.q: Why does drinking tea or coffee with meals reduce iron absorption?
faq.a: Tea and coffee contain tannins and polyphenols that bind tightly to dietary iron in your digestive tract, blocking up to 60% of iron absorption. Drink tea at least one hour away from meals.

faq.q: How long does it take for iron supplements to raise hemoglobin?
faq.a: Oral iron supplements usually increase hemoglobin within 2 to 4 weeks. However, doctors advise continuing therapy for 3 to 6 months to completely refill depleted ferritin stores.

articles.overview: Transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, dengue fever is an acute viral disease that causes severe symptoms nicknamed 'breakbone fever'. Understanding the 3 distinct phases of dengue—febrile, critical, and recovery—and diligently tracking blood platelet counts can save lives.
keyPoints: Febrile Phase (Days 1-5): Sudden high fever (103°F-105°F), retro-orbital eye pain, severe joint and back pain. Test with Dengue NS1 Antigen
Critical Phase (Days 3-7): Fever drops, but capillary plasma leakage can occur. Daily CBC Platelet Count monitoring is essential
Platelet drop: Platelets under 100,000 require close physician monitoring. Under 20,000 requires hospitalization and possible transfusion
Severe warning signs: Persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, gum or nose bleeding, extreme lethargy, and black stools
Hydration is key: Drink plenty of ORS, coconut water, and soups to maintain plasma volume

faq.q: Why is the day the fever subsides often the most dangerous in dengue?
faq.a: During the 'critical phase' when fever drops, vascular permeability can cause internal fluid leakage into lungs or abdomen, leading to a sudden plunge in platelets and blood pressure shock. Strict observation is vital on days 4 to 7.

faq.q: Can papaya leaf juice increase platelets in dengue?
faq.a: Papaya leaf extract has shown modest benefits in some clinical trials, but it must NEVER replace medical hydration, doctor supervision, and regular laboratory platelet monitoring.

Fast properly if instructed: 10-12 hours for lipid/full body, 8-10 hours for fasting sugar. No tea, coffee, or snacks.
Get a good night's rest: Poor sleep can temporarily spike blood pressure and stress hormones.
Keep your arms warm: Warm skin increases blood flow to surface veins, making blood collection effortless.

faq.q: I am afraid of needles. What should I do during the blood draw?
faq.a: Tell your phlebotomist! Our staff are trained to help nervous patients. Look away toward the ceiling, take slow, deep breaths, and relax your arm completely. The vacuum collection needle takes less than 10 seconds.

faq.q: Should I keep pressing the puncture site after the phlebotomist leaves?
faq.a: Apply firm, steady pressure with the cotton ball for 3 to 5 minutes without rubbing. Avoid lifting heavy weights with that arm for an hour to prevent minor bruising.
